pleiades.blurb: The Pleiades, also known as the Seven Sisters, is an open star cluster in the constellation Taurus.
pleiades.fact: It contains over 1,000 stars held together by gravity, many of which formed at the same time.

m101.blurb: M101, also known as the Pinwheel Galaxy, is a large spiral galaxy in the constellation Ursa Major.
m101.fact: Its bright spiral arms contain gas and dust, with regions where new stars are forming.

beehive.blurb: The Beehive Cluster (M44) is an open star cluster in the constellation Cancer.
beehive.fact: Its stars appear grouped together like a swarm of bees.

ecliptic0.blurb: This point is where the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path across the sky, crosses the celestial equator at the March (vernal) equinox.
ecliptic0.fact: It marks the beginning of right ascension, the celestial coordinate system's measure of east-west position.

ecliptic180.blurb: The ecliptic point at right ascension (RA) 180° is the September equinox.
ecliptic180.fact: At this point on the celestial sphere, the Sun's apparent path (the ecliptic) crosses the celestial equator as it moves from north to south.

galactic_center.blurb: The galactic center is the dynamical center of a galaxy, with a massive black hole surrounded by clusters of massive stars, such as those near Sgr A* in the Milky Way.
galactic_center.fact: It is a unique environment for star formation, and because dust dims its light so strongly (high extinction), it has to be studied in infrared.

north_pole.blurb: The North Ecliptic Pole is the point on the celestial sphere, in the constellation Draco, that lies directly north of the ecliptic plane.
north_pole.fact: Its counterpart, the South Ecliptic Pole, lies diametrically opposite, in the constellation Dorado.

south_pole.blurb: The South Ecliptic Pole is the point in the sky 90° south of the ecliptic, directly below the plane of the solar system.
south_pole.fact: It lies close to the Large Magellanic Cloud, in the constellation Dorado.
